original_question: Let gamma_k=1/(k+1)^(k+1). Determine whether the sequence {gamma_k/k!}_{k>=0}={1/((k+1)^(k+1)k!)}_{k>=0} is a multiplier sequence, and determine whether it is a complex zero decreasing sequence.
target_in_paper: Section 5, Problem 7 in “Scholia and open problems”: let gamma_k = 1/(k+1)^(k+1) for k in N_0, and determine whether the sequence {gamma_k/k!}_{k>=0} is (a) a multiplier sequence and (b) a complex zero decreasing sequence (CZDS). ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the exact sequence, the exact normalization by k!, and the paper’s two-part objective almost verbatim: decide whether {gamma_k/k!} is a multiplier sequence and whether it is a CZDS. This is essentially Problem 7 itself. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
missing_details: The paper uses the term classical multiplier sequence (of the first kind), not a more general basis-dependent notion.
The ambient space is the real polynomial ring R[x].
The relevant diagonal operator should be named explicitly: T[x^k] = (gamma_k/k!) x^k for k >= 0.
For the multiplier-sequence part, the quantifier is: for every real polynomial p(x) with only real zeros, T[p(x)] also has only real zeros.
For the CZDS part, the quantifier is: for every real polynomial p(x), Z_C(T[p]) <= Z_C(p), where Z_C(p) is the number of non-real zeros of p, counted with multiplicity.
The indexing set is k in N_0 = {0,1,2,...}.

The nearby context explains why the paper asks about the composed sequence gamma_k/k! rather than {gamma_k}: the unreweighted generating function psi(x) = sum_{k>=0} gamma_k x^k is stated not to belong to L-P^+.
No degree restriction, homogeneity assumption, nilpotency condition, or 'for sufficiently large' qualifier is part of this problem.
refined_question: Let gamma_k := 1/(k+1)^(k+1) for k in N_0, and let T: R[x] -> R[x] be the diagonal linear operator defined by T[x^k] := (gamma_k/k!) x^k = x^k/((k+1)^(k+1) k!). Determine whether the sequence {gamma_k/k!}_{k=0}^infinity is a classical multiplier sequence; that is, whether T[p] has only real zeros whenever p in R[x] has only real zeros. Also determine whether {gamma_k/k!}_{k=0}^infinity is a complex zero decreasing sequence, meaning that Z_C(T[p]) <= Z_C(p) for every p in R[x], where Z_C counts non-real zeros with multiplicity.
equivalent_formulation: Equivalent formulation for part (a) only: by the Pólya-Schur characterization in Theorem 2 together with Definition 2, since all terms are positive, asking whether {gamma_k/k!}_{k=0}^infinity is a multiplier sequence is equivalent to asking whether the entire function F(x) = sum_{k=0}^infinity x^k/((k+1)^(k+1)(k!)^2) belongs to the Laguerre-Pólya class of type I, equivalently to L-P^+. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
justification: The draft is targeting Problem 7, not the earlier problems in the paper. Section 5 states this open problem explicitly after Theorem 21, with exactly the same sequence gamma_k = 1/(k+1)^(k+1) and the same two questions: multiplier sequence and CZDS. The nearby introductory definitions supplying the hidden assumptions are Definition 3 (CZDS) and Definition 4 (multiplier sequence), both formulated for diagonal operators on real polynomials. Theorem 2 is the paper’s cited Pólya-Schur characterization, which supplies the paper-approved equivalent reformulation for the multiplier-sequence part. The same nearby Section 5 discussion also notes that psi(x) = sum gamma_k x^k is not in L-P^+, clarifying that the intended question is specifically about the composed sequence {gamma_k/k!}, not about {gamma_k} itself. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
